It used to be different.
Contracts used to arrive on paper.
A courier would bring them twice a week.
I used to spend three days a week in front of clients.
The fleet used to be half the size it is now.
That photograph on the wall behind you? That is this office in 2004. Those shelves used to be full of folders, one for every corporate client.
I have walked past it a hundred times and never asked. How did the contracts arrive, before the portal?
On paper. A courier would bring them twice a week, and we would file them by hand. If a client called about a fare, you walked to the shelf and read him the answer.
That sounds slow.
It was slow, and I am not nostalgic. Nobody wants the courier back. But everybody used to know where the paper trail was, and now half of it lives in a legacy system two countries still use.
So what do you actually miss? Not the paper, I imagine.
One habit. When the folder was on the shelf, you would open it and see the whole client. Twice a week, problem or no problem. That habit died out, and nothing replaced it.
I think I take that for granted. On the screen I only ever look at the invoice somebody is asking me about.

Before we start the training, a short story, because it explains why the system looks the way it does. Twenty years ago there were no corporate portals. Every contract used to arrive on paper, and a courier would bring it to the office twice a week. The account manager used to keep a folder for each client, and if a client called with a question about a fare, she would open the folder and read the answer from a printed page. It sounds slow, and it was. But everybody knew where the paper trail was, and nobody used to lose a contract in a system nobody had access to. That is the part we are still trying to get back.

People ask me what has really changed in this industry in twenty years, and they expect me to say technology. It is not technology. What changed is the amount of time. I used to spend three days a week in front of clients. Three days. I would drive to their office, sit down, drink coffee, and leave two hours later knowing something that was not in any report. Today I have the same number of clients and I see them twice a month, and the rest of the relationship happens on a screen. We used to say that this business was about aircraft. It never was. It used to be about who picked up the phone at six in the evening, and honestly, it still is.
